drop/recall: Take the recurrence with one unit, so every weight is a single number, and drop the tan-aitch and the bias.
drop/linear: What is left is h t equals a times h t minus one, plus b times x t: a linear recurrence. a, the decay, scales the old state. b, the input weight, scales the input.
drop/out: An output weight, c, reads out the output: y t equals c times h t. Here a is a half, and b and c are two.
drop/h1: From h zero at zero, read three, one, two. Step one: half of zero, plus two times three: six.
drop/h23: Step two: half of six, plus two, is five. Step three: half of five, plus four, is six point five, and y three is two times that: thirteen.
unroll/open: Now open the loop: put h two into h three, then h one, and the state becomes a sum of past inputs.
unroll/weights: Each input enters times b, then is multiplied by a for each step it waits. So the input k steps back weighs c, times a to the k, times b: four, two, one. Four times two, plus two, plus three: thirteen.
unroll/fade: Those weights are powers of a. With a at a half, they halve at every step back: old inputs fade.
unroll/blow: At one they hold; at two they double, and the state blows up. The size of a, written a between bars, decides: below one fades, above one blows up. A negative a only flips the sign.
parallel/seq: The tan-aitch recurrence cannot open like that: with a tan-aitch between steps, h two must wait for h one, and h three for h two.
parallel/all: Here, the weights are known before any input arrives. Every output is a weighted sum of the inputs, so all of them can be computed at once.
parallel/slide: Each row is the same weights, slid one step along: a convolution. That is why it trains in parallel, and why state space models such as S4 build on it.
try/p1: Try one: a is a half, b is four, from zero. Inputs two, one, three. What is h three?
try/a1: Eight. Then four plus four, eight. Then four plus twelve: sixteen.
try/p2: Now a is a half, b three, c two. What weight does y t give x t minus two?
try/a2: Two steps back: c, times a squared, times b. Two times a quarter times three: one point five.
